clinicalPearls: C2 deficiency is the commonest inherited complement deficiency in people of European ancestry and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
Many individuals are asymptomatic, but there is an increased risk of invasive infection with encapsulated organisms, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae.
It is associated with autoimmune disease, particularly a lupus-like syndrome that is often photosensitive but tends to be milder and less renal-predominant than C1q-related lupus.
The classical-pathway assay (CH50) is markedly reduced or absent while the alternative-pathway assay (AH50) is normal.
A specific low C2 level confirms the diagnosis once an isolated classical-pathway defect is identified.
A common two base-pair deletion (type I deficiency) accounts for most cases in populations of European descent.
Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination is central to management, alongside prompt treatment of febrile illness.
Because the alternative and lectin pathways remain intact, infections are generally less severe than in terminal-pathway defects.
reference.pathophysiology: C2 is a component shared by the classical and lectin complement pathways; it is cleaved to form the C3 convertase that amplifies complement activation. In C2 deficiency these pathways cannot efficiently generate C3 convertase, impairing opsonisation and clearance of encapsulated bacteria and predisposing to invasive pneumococcal disease. Reduced classical-pathway function also compromises the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic material, promoting autoantibody formation and a lupus-like syndrome. Because the alternative pathway is preserved and can still be triggered directly on microbial surfaces, residual complement activity persists, which is why many individuals remain asymptomatic and infections are usually less severe than in complete terminal-pathway deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Specific antibody or other primary immunodeficiency with recurrent pneumococcal infection
Acquired hypocomplementaemia from active immune-complex disease
additionalInvestigations: CH50 classical-pathway haemolytic assay (low or absent)
Genetic testing for the common C2 deletion
Autoimmune serology including ANA where a lupus-like syndrome is suspected
Vaccination status and functional antibody responses
Documentation of invasive infection history and organisms
redFlags: Recurrent severe or unusual bacterial infections
Signs of meningitis or fulminant sepsis
Failure to mount protective responses to vaccination
reference.prognosis: Many individuals lead normal lives, but there is a lifelong increased risk of invasive encapsulated-organism infection and of developing a usually milder lupus-like autoimmune disease. Vaccination and prompt antibiotic treatment markedly reduce infective mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming that being asymptomatic excludes the deficiency, as penetrance is variable.
Failing to prioritise pneumococcal and other encapsulated-organism vaccination.
Interpreting a low CH50 without confirming which component is deficient.
Overlooking C2 deficiency as an underlying cause of a lupus-like syndrome.
Delaying antibiotics in a febrile deficient patient while awaiting confirmation.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition
management: Immunise against encapsulated organisms with pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcal conjugate vaccines to compensate for impaired opsonisation.
Treat febrile or suspected invasive illness promptly with empirical antibiotics active against Streptococcus pneumoniae, without waiting for confirmation.
Consider prophylactic penicillin in those with recurrent invasive pneumococcal infection.
Manage the associated photosensitive lupus-like syndrome with sun protection, hydroxychloroquine and immunosuppression proportionate to disease activity.
Monitor for emergent autoimmune disease with periodic autoimmune serology and renal surveillance.
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and screen affected siblings.
Educate patient and family to seek urgent review with any fever, given the lifelong invasive-infection risk.
